answer: Resource/capacity isolation remains. Correct tenant-scoped data permissions control which records a tenant may read or write, but they do not stop one tenant's workload from consuming or starving the shared connection pool and delaying other tenants (noisy-neighbour effects / connection-pool starvation). The book treats compute and resource isolation as a separate axis from identity and data isolation, warns that equal CPU limits alone do not prevent shared storage or connection-pool starvation, and says a shared pool with tenant-scoped predicates is cheaper at low scale only with explicit fairness and escape hatches; a shared pool can strand capacity or fail to enforce quotas, so dedicated resources are justified when measured noisy-neighbour cost (or compliance risk) dominates. At the connection level, pooled reuse also carries session-scoped state (session settings, temporary objects, prepared statements, LISTEN/NOTIFY and locks), so tenant/session context must not be assumed to persist across checkouts.
